newsitem.title: USA: TWA churns managers in its turnaround struggle.
newsitem.headline: TWA churns managers in its turnaround struggle.

text.p: Trans World Airlines Inc's top management remains in flux as the carrier struggles for a turnaround.
TWA's short-term prospects will remain under pressure until the airline improves its service, strengthens its management team and sharpens its market focus, analysts said.
TWA said Friday Edward Soule resigned as chief financial officer after just four months on the job. Soule came to TWA after serving as a partner at Edward D. Jones & Co.
At the time, Wall Street viewed the choice of an outsider as a move toward strength and innovation.
Now, TWA shuffles Michael Palumbo, TWA's former vice president and treasurer, into Soule's slot and the airline keeps searching for a permanent chief executive.
"Perhaps they decided they didn't have time to get someone up to speed on the industry," said Glenn Engel, an analyst with Goldman Sachs. "Or maybe he (Soule) decided the job was too tough."
The pilots' union suggested Soule left because he was chosen by outgoing chief executive Jeffrey Erickson.
"Soule came in as Jeff's choice. He's leaving with Jeff. It was not unexpected," said Don Jacobs, a spokesman for the pilot's union.
The management changes may make TWA's turnaround more difficult, analysts said.

Earlier in the week, TWA named board member Gerald Gitner as vice chairman and acting chief executive officer. TWA tapped a temporary CEO after unsuccessfully courting several other airline executives, the pilot's union said.
"It shows that the chief executive job is not highly sought after. It's a tough position to fill since there's a lot of work to be done," Engel said.
"It's taking longer than planned to find a new top man," Jacobs said.
The short tenure of Soule and the difficulty in attracting a new chief executive to replace Jeffrey Erickson, who is leaving in January, signal deep problems at the carrier, analysts said.
TWA's third quarter results were hard hit by the fatal crash of Flight 800 in July. But some analysts said soft bookings after the crash only added to exisiting woes.
During the third quarter, TWA fumbled in its attempt to aggressively expand it summer flying schedule.
Over the past year, the airline also wasted efforts trying to bolster operations in unsuccessful markets such as JFK International Airport, analysts said.
TWA recently said it will back off from JFK and reduce international operations.
The St. Louis-based airline is now developing its 1997 operating plan and is expected to shift towards smaller planes for short-haul routes.
